source.title: Looking in the Mirror: Introspecting Side-Effect Misalignments Induced by Fine-Tuning
source.authors: K. Yoshida; Laura Gomezjurado Gonzalez; Yukinori Yamamoto; Yuji Naraki; Ryotaro Shimizu; Wen-Ya Wang

record.tranche_reason: It measures harmful-compliance score shifts between source models and existing fine-tuned PEFT adapters, using post-hoc safety evaluations rather than a controlled fine-tuning intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates fine-tuned models on safety benchmarks and reports shifts in harmful compliance; those findings bear on V2. Its activation-patching analysis concerns how introspection adapters form safer/riskier judgments, not how the models produce harmful responses. Table 2 and Figure 1 compare introspection-reporting methods and are not results on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study scores harmful compliance (HEx-PHI 1–5 rubric, LLM judge) of 213 downloaded PEFT adapters for Qwen3-14B and Gemma3-12B-it against their source models. Its Appendix C.1 reports per-category shifts. That is a result on V2 (fine-tuning not aimed at harm raising harmful compliance), but in an uncontrolled in-the-wild setting rather than with a fixed benign recipe, so it is T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The paper's main conclusion is that introspection adapters, especially DAIA, generalise out of distribution in reporting alignment shifts. The fine-tuning safety result is secondary: shifts arise often, mostly in the riskier direction, but vary widely by category, model family and adapter (copyright gets safer).
record.recipe_differences: Uses downloaded, heterogeneous PEFT adapters and post-hoc harmful-compliance evaluations; it does not control the fine-tuning data or reproduce a few-example fine-tuning procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported alignment shifts vary by category, adapter, and source-model family. The authors also report that standard deviations exceed mean shifts in many categories.
record.problems: The fine-tuning adapters are heterogeneous and their data and objectives are not controlled for this analysis, so the results do not isolate benign-data effects or establish a causal effect for a particular training recipe. Harmful-compliance scoring uses an LLM judge. Category-level prompt counts vary, with some categories having relatively few prompts.
record.rows_left_out: Individual category-by-model-family values from Figures 3–4 are not separately transcribed: the extracted figure layout does not unambiguously assign all displayed means and standard deviations to their category and model-family pairs. The paper discusses their heterogeneity in Appendix C.1.

untested.parts: No controlled harmful-example fine-tuning or example counts. A few adapters (e.g. insecure-code, jailbreak-classifier) are pooled with others and not analysed separately.

Does not verify the adapters' training data as benign or control the recipe. It does not test 'carefully chosen' benign data. The pool includes safety-training adapters (thinksafe, direct-refusal) that would bias toward safer. It reports no refusal or attack-success rates.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested. The activation patching concerns introspection judgments, not safety behaviour.

missing.what: Per-category mean ± SD harmful-compliance shifts for each family, e.g. Qwen Disinfo +0.25±0.50, Cyber +0.14±0.36, Fraud +0.14±0.37; Gemma Cyber +0.14±0.41, Disinfo −0.02±0.46, Financial −0.04±0.53. These are legible for categories 1–10, so rows_left_out's claim that they are ambiguous is only partly right.
Composition of the adapter pool: it includes explicit safety-training adapters and insecure-code / poisoning adapters, so it is not a purely benign set. This matters for reading V2.

record.verdict_notes: The shift scale is a 1–5 judge score, not a compliance rate, so magnitudes are not comparable to Qi et al.'s attack-success numbers. Qwen3-14B is the post-trained (hybrid-thinking) release, so 'base' in the record means source model, not pretrained base. No capability check was run. The judge is GPT-5.6 Luna at temperature 1.0.

versions.untested_parts: Does not isolate harmful-example fine-tuning, report harmful-example counts, or test whether a few to a few hundred such examples remove refusal.

Does not isolate ordinary or carefully chosen benign training data as a controlled condition, or report refusal rates; evaluates heterogeneous existing PEFT adapters and category-level harmful-compliance score shifts.
No test of compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes on harmful-completion rates.
Does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behavior; its adapter ablations concern introspection performance.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate methods for deepening safety across response tokens.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B fine-tuned models (121 adapters; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: base model with fine-tuned PEFT adapters
rows.operation_detail: Compared category-level harmful-compliance scores of fine-tuned adapters with their corresponding source model; aggregate finding across categories and adapters.

conditions.value: StrongREJECT, HarmBench, HEx-PHI, and AdvBench prompts

rows.measure: Change in category-level misalignment score; higher scores indicate greater harmful compliance.
rows.value: Average shifts were positive in many categories; shifts varied substantially by category and adapter.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviations are reported for category-level shifts in Figure 3; no single aggregate uncertainty stated here.
rows.note: The paper states that positive shifts mean greater vulnerability to harmful requests. This is an aggregate textual finding, not a single pooled numerical estimate.
rows.check: Readable Figure 3 means for Qwen3-14B are about +0.06 to +0.25 on a 1–5 scale in 9 of 10 visible categories (Privacy −0.01). SDs (0.18–0.51) exceed the means. Most shifts fall in the paper's 'slightly riskier' band (0.08–0.60), so the effect is a small move. The value should cite these numbers rather than prose only.

source_check.correct: The Qwen3-14B pool has positive average harmful-compliance shifts in many categories, with substantial variation. Its adapters' training data are not established as benign; versions should be ["none"] and state cannot_determine for V2.
source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.2 and 5.1; Appendix B, Table 8; Appendix C.1, Figures 3–4.
source_check.problem: The aggregate shift is correctly recorded, but unverified training data prevent interpreting it as a partial V2 effect.

relation.reason: Benign fine-tuning safety erosion motivates the work and is discussed through prior studies; this study's own pooled results do not identify the benign-data condition required by V2.

tranche.reason: The reported pools measure harmful-compliance changes after heterogeneous adaptation, without establishing benign training or reporting a verified benign subset. They therefore do not test V2 as worded. The introspection experiments do not test another listed version.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv:2608.04347v2, titled Introspecting Alignment Shifts Beyond Behaviors Implanted Through Fine-Tuning; the pack uses a different title. Directional findings remain readable despite incomplete figure extraction.

statements.correction: Both downloaded adapter pools have safer copyright means; magnitudes are unreadable. Training-data benignness is unverified. These aggregates cannot isolate benign fine-tuning effects.
The study compares downloaded adapters against their source models, providing before/after score differences. It does not establish benign training data or isolate benign-data effects.
